list.listitem: Suspect hypersensitivity pneumonitis in patients with pulmonary symptoms associated with recent exposure to inhaled antigen (eg, thermophilic bacteria, fungi, animal proteins). C
Initial evaluation should include CXR, pulmonary function tests (PFTs), high-resolution CT, and antibodies to possible antigen exposures. Biopsy may be needed. C
Most patients recover with supportive treatment, but corticosteroids may improve short-term outcomes in more severely symptomatic patients. B
Most patients do well, although some residual pulmonary function impairment is common, and patients with chronic fibrotic disease have a poor prognosis. B

background.definition: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is an uncommon respiratory disease of immune etiology. It is also known as "farmer's lung" and is caused by inhalation of antigens to which the patient was previously sensitized. Antigens include animal proteins, fungi, and thermophilic bacteria. Other synonyms to HP include summer-type hypersensitivity pneumonitis, air conditioner lung, humidifier lung, and pigeon breeder's lung (budgerigar fancier's lung).

list.listitem: Approximately 5% to 15% of exposed population develop HP; 8% of pigeon handlers and 4.3% of farmers can develop HP.
Approximately 45% of lung transplant recipients develop bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia within 5 years.
More than 300 antigens have been identified, which is the major risk factor for disease (OR 38.8).
Farmer's lung is the most common occupational cause resulting from inhalation of toxic antigens such as mouldy hay.
Recreational sources include aerosolized antigens from steam baths and saunas.
Avocational sources include bird handlers working with pigeons and other domestic poultry.
Other sources include industrial dusts from copper and plastic industries.
Environmental exposures (especially to mold in homes) is increasingly thought to be a risk factor.
Keep in mind that 25% of sources are unidentifiable.

The inciting antigen causes lymphocytic activation and lymphokine release with other biochemical mediators causing the development of granulomas. Continued exposure causes fibroblast growth factor stimulation leading to irreversible fibrosis.
Etiologic basis includes both type 3 (immune complex) and type 4 (delayed) mechanisms of hypersensitivity.
Suspect HP in at-risk patients (eg, farmers, bird or mold exposure) with exertional dyspnea, nonproductive cough and/or inspiratory crackles. C

Order CXR (may show ground-glass appearance with a reticulonodular pattern), antigens to suspected exposure, and PFTs (restrictive pattern with diffusion abnormality). If not diagnostic, order high resolution CT. C

list.listitem: Consider HP in patients with cough, interstitial lung disease, and a concerning environmental, occupational, or avocational exposure. The initial presentation will typically include nonproductive cough with exertional dyspnea and hypoxia. At risk patients include farmers and bird fanciers, and settings may include damp basements and heated pools.

An observational study of 661 patients with HP identified key signs and symptoms of this disease. They include exposure to an offending agent (OR 39), presence of positive precipitating antibodies (OR 5.3), recurrent episodes of symptoms (OR 3.3), inspiratory crackles (OR 4.5), symptoms 4 to 8 hours after exposure (OR 7.2), and weight loss (OR 2.0).
On physical examination, patients may have bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation. There are no signs of consolidation in most cases. Digital clubbing a late and poor prognostic sign.

HP is classified into acute, subacute, and chronic forms. These presentations depend on the duration and intensity of exposure. For example, intense antigenic exposure is seen in pigeon handlers, compared with a more limited exposure in bird fanciers.
Acute onset: presents with symptoms 2 to 9 hours after exposure, peaking at 24 hours, and subsiding by 48 hours.
Subacute presentation: the patient has a semiproductive cough and exertional dyspnea over many weeks.
Chronic: the chronic form may present with progressive shortness of breath without acute flare-ups and increasing hypoxemia.

Initial testing should include a CXR, PFTs, and antibody tests to suspected antigens. PFTs typically demonstrate a mixed restrictive and diffusional defect. Patients may have hypoxemia, especially after exercise. CXR will reveal a ground-glass attenuation and reticulonodular pattern, sometimes accompanied by hilar lymphadenopathy. IgG serum antibodies may precipitate with offending antigen.

British CHEST guidelines (2021) recommend that high resolution computed tomography should be ordered. It should not be used alone to make the diagnosis, but should be used in conjunction with the clinical presentatino. This usually shows ground-glass attenuation and diffuse peribronchial/centrilobular nodules less than 5 mm diameter. It is also useful for classifying patients as with or without fibrosis.

Guidelines recommend that BAL or biopsy should be reserved for situations where the diagnosis remains uncertain after the above evluation. If obtained, BAL usually reveals fluid that is lymphocyte rich with a predomination of CD8+ T cells. Macrophages secreting chemokines are present. Lung biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and can be performed using video assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open lung biopsy. These reveal interstitial noncaseating granulomas and mononuclear giant cells with or without fibrosis.
Patients may have elevated serum markers of inflammation, eg, ESR, CRP, ferritin, or lactate dehydrogenase. However, these findings are nonspecific.
Serum antigen-specific IgG/IgA should not be used to confirm or rule out the diagnosis. Antigen specific inhalation challenge testing is also not recommended by CHEST guidelines (2021).
Suspect HP in patients with a concerning history (ie, bird exposure, mold exposure, farming) who present with nonproductive cough or dyspnea. May be acute, subacute, or chronic.
When HP suspected order a CXR (which may show ground glass or reticulonodular changes), pulmonary function tests, and antibodies to suspected antigens.

Proposed diagnostic criteria include: (1) clinical evaluation and pulmonary function tests indicate an interstitial lung disease, (2) the CXR is consistent, (3) there is exposure to a recognized cause, and (4) there is antibody to that antigen.
If nondiagnostic, order high resolution CT. Definitive testing includes BAL and/or lung biopsy; however, this is rarely needed.
Remove patient from the offending allergen if possible, or provide respiratory protection. C
Consider corticosteroids for patients with severe disease, although this does not change long-term outcomes. B
Initial symptomatic relief may include bronchodilators and mucolytics for wheezing.
Macrolides have been used mainly for their anti inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in subacute HP.
Consider corticosteroids for patients with severe disease. Typical dosing is 40 to 60 mg/d with a taper over 4 to 8 weeks.

A single small RCT with 36 patients with farmer's lung found that those treated with steroids had a somewhat faster recovery of lung function but no long-term difference in pulmonary function, recurrence, or symptoms.
In patients diagnosed with HP, immediate intervention includes cessation of exposure to inciting antigens.
If that is not possible, provide respiratory protection.
Provide oxygen as needed acutely.
Patients may benefit from referral to a pulmonologist and/or allergist if they have more severe disease or if the cause is unclear.
Acute, mild disease: if symptoms appear 4 to 8 hours after exposure, removal from offending environment with supportive therapy often leads to resolution within 48 hours. C
A 5-year follow-up of 86 patients with farmer's lung found that recovery plateaued at 6 months, that most had some respiratory symptoms, but that two-thirds were able to return to work. B

In a long-term follow-up of 89 patients with farmer's lung and 86 matched controls, cases had similar vital capacity and FEV1 as controls, but were more likely to have evidence of airway obstruction. B
Patients with chronic ongoing constant exposure may have progressive deterioration of pulmonary function with fibrotic lung tissue changes; this has a poor prognosis. B
